Plan a break from work: map the income drop and the reserve before you leave

Follow temporary income, household spending and the cash reserve through a planned absence, then solve the additional saving required before it begins.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a planned break from work

Interactive planning lab

Starting fund required$18,000
Additional saving needed$3,000
Monthly saving before the break$250

Hypothetical planned absence beginning today after a preparation phase. All monthly spending and income inputs are net cash amounts. Upfront costs occur before month 1; income and spending occur at month-end. Temporary income ends after the entered number of months, even if the absence continues. No interest, inflation, program entitlement, pension accrual, job protection, employer conditions or extra return-to-work costs are calculated. This is not an EI, QPIP or employer-benefit estimator.

The central idea

A planned work break needs a dated income schedule. Fund the lowest cumulative cash position, including upfront costs and the months after temporary payments end.

01

Start with the cash the household will actually receive

A planned absence can involve parenting, study, caregiving or another life transition. Begin with the household’s continuing income, any temporary payments and the spending that remains due. The Financial Consumer Agency of Canada’s budget guidance includes planning for life events and reviewing income, expenses and savings together.

All income inputs here are net cash amounts, after any tax or payroll deductions you expect to apply. Continuing income remains throughout the break. Temporary income arrives for the selected number of months, then stops even if the absence continues.

The model does not assume that taking time away creates eligibility for a benefit. For parental leave, the Government of Canada’s EI information explains that amounts and duration depend on the applicable program and circumstances, and that some employers provide top-ups. Confirm the actual arrangement before entering the cash-flow schedule.

02

Put the end of temporary income on the chart

The default household spends CAD 4,500 per month, receives CAD 2,500 of continuing monthly income and adds CAD 1,500 of temporary income for six months. Its first six monthly shortfalls are CAD 500 each. After the temporary payments end, the shortfall rises to CAD 2,000 a month.

The income chart marks that change against the spending line. The two inputs have different roles: the length of the break controls how long expenses continue, while the temporary-income duration controls when that payment stops. Extending one does not automatically extend the other.

Actual paydays, benefit processing, employer conditions and return-to-work timing can differ from a simple monthly schedule. A detailed plan should use confirmed payment dates and include any gap before the first receipt. The calculator assumes all monthly cash flows occur at month-end and does not estimate program eligibility, withholding or job-protected leave rights.

03

Fund the worst cumulative position

The reserve model begins by paying the entered upfront costs before month one. It then adds monthly income and subtracts spending. The required starting fund is the amount that keeps the lowest cumulative position at or above zero.

For the default twelve-month break, CAD 3,000 of upfront costs plus six CAD 500 gaps and six CAD 2,000 gaps require CAD 18,000 at the start. With CAD 15,000 allocated, the additional saving requirement is CAD 3,000. Spreading that over twelve preparation months gives CAD 250 a month, with no interest assumed.

Funding the lowest point matters even if the full period eventually produces a surplus. Upfront payments may need cash before later income arrives. Conversely, early monthly surpluses can help fund later shortfalls if that money remains available. The model retains both effects rather than simply adding every negative month while ignoring the positive ones.

04

Compare the reserve path with the annual-style total

The cash-balance chart shows the currently allocated savings and the fully funded starting reserve. A line below zero identifies spending that needs another funding source. It does not represent approved credit or include the cost of borrowing to fill the gap.

The waterfall adds upfront and ongoing spending, then subtracts continuing income, temporary payments and allocated savings. A positive endpoint means a net shortfall by the final month; a negative endpoint means a surplus. Because it summarizes the full period, read it alongside the monthly path to catch any earlier shortage.

The matrix changes the break’s duration and temporary monthly income while keeping the selected duration of those payments fixed. Each cell reruns the timing calculation and shows the additional fund required after allocated savings. Its income levels are hypothetical alternatives, not statutory benefit rates or employer offers.

05

Include the transition back into the household plan

The calculator leaves several items for a wider review: pension accrual, workplace insurance, employer top-up conditions, tuition, care costs, work-related savings, tax changes and costs on returning to work. Identify which are already included in spending and which need separate dated amounts.

Check the consequence of a longer absence or a delayed restart of earnings. Also keep an emergency reserve distinct from the savings deliberately assigned to the break. A plan that uses every accessible dollar for known costs has less room for an unrelated shock.

Before the break begins, reconcile the confirmed income schedule, planned expenses, available savings and preparation transfers. The calculated monthly saving amount must fit the current budget; it does not establish affordability by itself. Update the schedule as arrangements become definite, and review it again when the actual cash flows start.
